## Solution

Let $\lambda = \mu + \nu$. Since $f = \frac{d\mu}{d\lambda}$ and $\mu \le \lambda$, we have $0 \le f \le 1$ $\lambda$-a.e. The Radon–Nikodym derivative of $\nu$ with respect to $\lambda$ is

$$g := \frac{d\nu}{d\lambda} = \frac{d(\lambda - \mu)}{d\lambda} = 1 - f.$$

For any measurable set $A$,

$$\nu(A) = \int_A g\,d\lambda = \int_A (1-f)\,d\lambda.$$

Now compute $\nu(\{x : f(x) < 1\})$:

$$\nu(\{f < 1\}) = \int_{\{f < 1\}} (1-f)\,d\lambda.$$

Since $f \le 1$ $\lambda$-a.e., the set $\{f > 1\}$ has $\lambda$-measure $0$, and on $\{f = 1\}$ we have $(1-f) = 0$. Therefore

$$\int_{\{f < 1\}} (1-f)\,d\lambda = \int_{\Omega} (1-f)\,d\lambda - \int_{\{f=1\}} (1-f)\,d\lambda = \int_{\Omega} (1-f)\,d\lambda - 0.$$

Hence

$$\nu(\{f < 1\}) = \int_{\Omega} (1-f)\,d\lambda = \int_{\Omega} g\,d\lambda = \nu(\Omega) = 2.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
